claims.claim: The figure was a ten-foot stone man found in a well pit.
claims.quote: It was a 10-foot-tall (3.0 m), roughly 3,000 pound purported "petrified man", uncovered on October 16, 1869, by workers digging a well behind the barn of William C. "Stub" Newell, in Cardiff, New York.

claims.claim: The discovery took place at Cardiff, New York, in October 1869.
claims.quote: uncovered on October 16, 1869, by workers digging a well behind the barn of William C. "Stub" Newell, in Cardiff, New York

claims.claim: The photograph of the giant is a Bain News Service image dated 1910, public domain.
claims.quote:
Date: 1910
Author: Bain News Service, publisher
Licence: Public domain

claims.claim: Two men hired to dig a well found the giant.
claims.quote: Newell hired Gideon Emmons and Henry Nichols, ostensibly to dig a well, and on October 16, 1869, they found the giant.

claims.claim: One of the men reportedly said, "I declare, some old Indian has been buried here!"
claims.quote: One of the men reportedly exclaimed, "I declare, some old Indian has been buried here!"

claims.claim: A printed lithograph presented the figure with a list of measurements.
claims.quote: ITS DIMENSIONS ARE Whole length of the figure, 10 feet, 4½ inches; from crown of head to chin, 1 foot, 9 inches; length of nose, 6 inches

claims.claim: The listed length of the nose was six inches.
claims.quote: length of nose, 6 inches

claims.claim: The listed width of the palm was seven inches.
claims.quote: width of palm, 7 inches

claims.claim: The print was titled "The Onondaga Giant."
claims.quote: THE ONONDAGA GIANT. EXHUMED AT CARDIFF, ONONDAGA CO., N. Y., OCT. 16, 1869.

claims.claim: The print was sold (offered for sale) under that name.
claims.quote: Entered according to Act of Congress, in the year 1869, by A. L. Edwards, in the Clerk's Office, of the District Court, for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania.

claims.claim: The lithograph is "The Onondaga Giant" by Popular Graphic Arts.
claims.quote: Archive title: File:The Onondaga giant LCCN2003666806.jpg ... Author: Popular Graphic Arts

claims.claim: The giant began as a block of gypsum.
claims.quote: Hull, accompanied by a man named H. B. Martin, hired men to quarry out a 10-foot-4.5-inch-long (3.2 m) block of gypsum in Fort Dodge, Iowa

claims.claim: The block was quarried in Iowa in 1868.
claims.quote: In 1868, Hull, accompanied by a man named H. B. Martin, hired men to quarry out a 10-foot-4.5-inch-long (3.2 m) block of gypsum in Fort Dodge, Iowa

claims.claim: The quarry workmen were told the block was intended for a monument to Abraham Lincoln.
claims.quote: telling them it was intended for a monument to Abraham Lincoln in New York

claims.claim: The stereocard shows Cardiff Glen, Fort Dodge, Iowa, 1873, from NYPL.
claims.quote: VIEW IN CARDIFF GLEN. NEAR FORT DODGE, IOWA.

claims.claim: The printed back of the stereocard names the hoaxers as George Hull and H. B. Martin.
claims.quote: The perpetrators of the imposture are well remembered by old residents of Fort Dodge. Their names were George Hull and H. B. Martin.

claims.claim: The card states the giant was carved in Chicago, buried in a barn lot, and subsequently "discovered."
claims.quote: The block was taken to Chicago, the "Giant" carved, and then shipped to the point in New York which gave it its name, where it was buried in a barn lot, and subsequently "discovered".

claims.claim: Hull confessed.
claims.quote: On December 10, 1869, Hull confessed everything to the press

claims.claim: Whether the Chicago stonecutter knew what was being carved is unresolved in the record; only the hanging of quilts to muffle the carving is noted.
claims.quote: While it is not clear if Burkhardt was aware of Hull's intentions, it is reported that they took steps to cover up their work during the carving, putting up quilts to lessen the sound of carving.

claims.claim: The well was being dug behind William Newell's barn.
claims.quote: uncovered on October 16, 1869, by workers digging a well behind the barn of William C. "Stub" Newell, in Cardiff, New York

claims.claim: George Hull was a New York tobacconist and a skeptic.
claims.quote: The giant was the creation of a New York tobacconist named George Hull.

claims.claim: Hull lost an argument at a Methodist revival meeting about the giants of Genesis 6:4.
claims.quote: Hull got into an argument with Reverend Turk and his supporters at a Methodist revival meeting about Genesis 6:4, which states that there were giants who once lived on Earth. Hull, a skeptic, being the minority party, lost the argument.

claims.claim: Hull set out to prove how easily people could be fooled.
claims.quote: Angered by his defeat and the credulity of people, Hull wanted to prove how easily he could fool people with a fake giant.

claims.claim: Hull shipped the block to a Chicago stonecutter named Edward Burkhardt.
claims.quote: He shipped the block to Edward Burkhardt in Chicago, a German stonecutter.

claims.claim: The giant was carved to imitate Hull's own body.
claims.quote: The giant was designed to imitate the form of Hull himself.

claims.claim: Hull learned from a geologist that hair does not petrify, so the giant has no hair or beard.
claims.quote: Hull consulted a geologist and learned that hairs would not be petrified, so he removed the hair and beard from the giant.

claims.claim: Sulphuric acid was used to age the surface.
claims.quote: The giant was also rubbed with sulphuric acid to create a deeper, vintage-like color.

claims.claim: Steel knitting needles embedded in a board were used to simulate pores.
claims.quote: The giant's surface was beaten with steel knitting needles embedded in a board to simulate pores.

claims.claim: Newell charged fifty cents for a fifteen-minute viewing.
claims.quote: the next day, a tent was set up on the discovery site and Newell charged each visitor fifty cents for a fifteen-minute session of viewing the giant.

claims.claim: Three to five hundred people visited per day.
claims.quote: The number of visitors went to about three to five hundred per day as the demand for wagons and carriages dramatically increased.

claims.claim: Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh noted soluble gypsum with fresh tool marks and called it "a most decided humbug."
claims.quote: Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh examined the statue, pointing out that it was made of soluble gypsum, which, had it been buried in its blanket of wet earth for centuries, would not still have fresh tool marks on it (which it did), and termed it "a most decided humbug".

claims.claim: Andrew D. White was associated with Cornell and questioned why anyone would dig a well in that spot.
claims.quote: Andrew D. White, the first president of Cornell University, made a close inspection of the Cardiff Giant. He noticed that there was no good reason to try to dig a well in the exact spot the giant had been found.

claims.claim: Hull confessed on December 10, 1869.
claims.quote: On December 10, 1869, Hull confessed everything to the press

claims.claim: The stereocard depicts the gypsum quarry from which the block was taken.
claims.quote: This is the Gypsum Quarry from which was taken the block out of which the original "Cardiff Giant" was carved.
